race.office: Governor of Alaska (open seat; Gov. Mike Dunleavy term-limited)

nominee.t: Advanced as the top Republican (3rd overall, 2nd among the four who advanced). Aug. 18, 2026 top-four nonpartisan primary (17 candidates, 164,303 votes): Kreiss-Tomkins 37,006 (22.5%); Begich 34,172 (20.8%, withdrew); Wilson 16,468 (10.0%); Bronson 13,364 (8.1%); Taylor 11,928 (7.3%); Bishop 11,527 (7.0%, withdrew). Running mate: state Sen. Mike Shower (R-Wasilla), Senate minority leader.

ballot.t: Four-candidate ranked-choice general ballot (Nov. 3, 2026): Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) / Zac Johnson; Bernadette Wilson (R) / Mike Shower; Dave Bronson (R) / Josh Church; Treg Taylor (R) / Candice English. Tom Begich (D, 2nd) withdrew Aug. 28 and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins; Click Bishop (R, 6th) also withdrew, which let Taylor (5th) advance. The Division of Elections' candidate list was updated after 11 p.m. Sept. 4 to show Taylor with English as running mate. First general ballots mailed starting Sept. 18.

oneliner.t: Republican business owner and conservative activist: majority owner of an Anchorage garbage company, former Alaska state director of Americans for Prosperity and former interim director of the Alaska Policy Forum, and a sponsor of the ballot effort to repeal ranked-choice voting.

born.t: c. 1983–84, Kenai, Alaska (her pamphlet statement gives age 42 and birthplace Kenai; exact date not found)

hometown.t: Born in Kenai; grew up in Anchorage (her own account)

upbringing.t: By her own account she was born in Kenai and raised in Anchorage. Her Aleut heritage runs through a grandmother born in Naknek, and she is a member of the Naknek Native Village Council. Alaska Public Media reports she is a great-niece of former Gov. Walter Hickel. She describes herself as a single mother of three. Her statement says her family has run Alaska businesses for more than 40 years.

career.role: Majority owner (75%; her mother Roberta Zipay owns 25%)
Senior advisor (her own account: Begich's 'second campaign')

platform.t: Restore the PFD by following the statutory formula, even if a small payout results ('Maybe it's only a $25 dividend, but follow the formula'). Favors putting the formula in the constitution.
No new taxes, including industry or income taxes. Wants a spending cap, audits, zero-based budgeting and a five-year rolling average. Earlier proposed shrinking the state workforce.
Calls industry 'not the enemy' and wants to restart shelved projects: Ambler, King Cove, ANWR, NPR-A, West Susitna and Juneau access.
Supported a significant increase in basic school funding (breaking with Dunleavy) and also education savings accounts.

Frames Anchorage's problem as drug and psychiatric rather than homelessness. Expand mental-health facilities, repeal certificate-of-need, allow interstate license transfer for mental-health providers. Says the governor should veto state money to Anchorage if results are not shown.
Opposes ranked-choice voting and is a sponsor of the initiative to repeal open primaries and RCV. Calls election integrity the foundation of the republic.

promises.t: Pay the PFD by the statutory formula and seek to put the formula in the constitution.
Oppose every new tax on industry or income.
Impose a spending cap and zero-based budgeting.
Withdraw if she finished behind another Republican in the primary (Sept. 2025 pledge).

record.t: The Beacon reports that paying the dividend under the 1982–2016 statutory formula would cost about $2 billion a year more than lawmakers and Dunleavy approved in 2025. So recent dividends have been set below the formula.

record.t: NAEP state rankings were not retrieved.

record.t: Budget totals for FY2027 were not retrieved; the June 2026 veto story gives only the $89.5M veto total.

said.t: Said she and Shower would withdraw and back the leading Republican if they finished behind another Republican in the primary, and called staying in after trailing 'very arrogant'.

did.t: Finished as the top Republican (10.0%), stayed in, and asked Bronson and Taylor to suspend their campaigns, calling them spoilers.

said.t: Campaigns on restoring a full, formula-based PFD.

did.t: Her own 2023 and 2024 PFDs were garnished to help satisfy a default judgment for unpaid fuel bills owed by her company and personally guaranteed by her. The judgment was satisfied Sept. 23, 2025. This is listed as context for her messaging, not as a contradiction of a policy promise.

saydo.note: Context only; the judgment is counted once, under legal record.

entries.t: Follow the statutory formula even if the result is small ('maybe only a $25 dividend').
Described by the Beacon as wanting to restore the older, more generous PFD formula; repeated 'follow the formula' at Sept. 21 forum.
Supports significant increase in basic school funding and education savings accounts.
Emphasizes poor reading/math rankings; no specific funding figure stated.
Sponsor of 2026 initiative to repeal open primaries and RCV.
'I don't support rank choice voting at all'; calls it confusing and discriminatory.

Court record details come from The Alaska Landmine, which linked Anchorage Superior Court filings (case 3AN-22-08465CI). An ADN story of Oct. 3, 2026 headlined that she 'has been sued repeatedly over unpaid bills' could not be opened (robots-blocked), so other cases it may describe are NOT recorded here. checks.claims: Campaign site bernadetteforgovernor.com could not be fetched (tool provenance block). As a stand-in, used her candidate-authored Official Election Pamphlet statement (bio and issue claims) and her KTUU 'On the Record' interview. Ad scripts were not found except a description of her 'Chat JKT' ad, which attacks Kreiss-Tomkins over AI-industry money; that ad was not rated because its exact claims were not available. Seven claims: 3 rated (true, partly, true), 4 unverifiable.
checks.democracy: Never held office. Searched news for statements on the 2020 or 2024 presidential results; none found. Her documented election-related statements concern RCV and election administration.

legal.t: Shoreside Petroleum sued Denali Disposal, Wilson personally (she had signed a 2020 personal guarantee on the fuel account) and her mother, Roberta Zipay over more than $52,000 in fuel debt (Anchorage Superior Court 3AN-22-08465CI, filed Oct. 2022). No defendant responded. A default judgment followed: $53,800 on Feb. 2, 2023, amended to $57,400 on May 3, 2023. Collection included bank sweeps and garnishment of her 2023 and 2024 PFDs. Two company checks from 2022 (about $5,400 and $13,000) were returned for insufficient funds; no criminal charge was reported.
